choices.misconception: I counted permutations where no number at all is in its own position, a full derangement of six, but positions 4, 5 and 6 have no restriction.
I subtracted the singles and added back the pairs but forgot to subtract the 6 permutations that fix all three of 1, 2 and 3.
I added the 6 permutations that fix all three numbers at the last step instead of subtracting them.
I read the conditions as saying not all three of 1, 2, 3 are fixed, so I only subtracted the 3! = 6 permutations fixing all of them.

hints: Count the permutations that break a rule, then subtract.
Let $E_i$ be the set of permutations with $p_i = i$ for $i = 1, 2, 3$. Use inclusion-exclusion on $|E_1 \cup E_2 \cup E_3|$.
Each single set has $5! = 120$ permutations, each pair $4! = 24$, and the triple $3! = 6$. So $|E_1 \cup E_2 \cup E_3| = 360 - 72 + 6 = 294$.

solutions.reliable: There are $720$ permutations in all. Let $E_i$ be those with $p_i = i$. Fixing one value leaves $5! = 120$ permutations, fixing two leaves $24$, and fixing three leaves $6$. By inclusion-exclusion, $|E_1 \cup E_2 \cup E_3| = 3 \cdot 120 - 3 \cdot 24 + 6 = 294$. The permutations obeying all three rules number $720 - 294 = 426$. Check by brute force (a short program over all $720$ permutations) or by a second count: choose $p_1, p_2, p_3$ so that none is fixed and fill the last three positions in $3! = 6$ ways; the number of valid triples $(p_1, p_2, p_3)$ of distinct values from $1$ to $6$ with $p_i \ne i$ is $71$, and $71 \cdot 6 = 426$. The idea: a rule of the form none of these happen is a job for complementary counting with inclusion-exclusion.
